title: The Environment Watchdog Under Pressure: OEP Priorities, Targets, and Enforcement (Corrected: 9 September 2026)
label: OEP priorities, targets & enforcement
summary: The Environment and Climate Change Committee questioned the Office for Environmental Protection (OEP) about its priorities, funding, and enforcement. The OEP warned that nature-friendly farming, water reform, marine protection, and waste are key concerns, but that government is still largely off track to meet legally binding environmental targets, including halting species decline by 2030. There was extensive discussion of the OEP's powers, the waste inspection report, the need for better data and delivery plans, and the challenge of policing environmental law when resources are tight.

chapters.title: New chair, old problems
chapters.takeaway: Dame Helen Ghosh sets out her priorities and admits the OEP faces a flat cash budget, which is a real-terms cut.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Dame Helen, you're new to the role. What are your plans and priorities?

turns.speaker: Dame Helen Ghosh
turns.text: The OEP is in good shape and has an excellent staff, but we're facing a big resource challenge. Our budget for the next three years is flat cash, which is effectively a real-terms cut. So we have to be really clear about what we prioritise.

turns.speaker: Dame Helen Ghosh
turns.text: My priorities are nature-friendly farming, water industry reform, and marine protection. In Northern Ireland, the big issue is nutrients from farming and sewage. We'll also keep an eye on planning.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You said you'll focus on areas that make the most difference. Which areas deserve priority?

turns.speaker: Dame Helen Ghosh
turns.text: Getting nature-friendly farming right is the single most important thing. That means sorting out support schemes, protected areas, and regulation. We're also looking at water reform to make sure past mistakes aren't repeated. Marine is a big area—we have an investigation into good environmental status.

chapters.title: Enforcement and working with others
chapters.takeaway: The OEP works closely with other regulators but is prepared to use tough powers when needed, though it has never yet taken a public body to court.

turns.speaker: Baroness Whitaker
turns.text: You're not the only body enforcing environmental rules. How do you work with others, and how do you prioritise enforcement?

turns.speaker: Dame Helen Ghosh
turns.text: We have clear powers under the Act. We're not the regulator of regulators, but we keep close to public authorities like Natural England, Ofwat, and the Environment Agency. We also work with the Climate Change Committee on adaptation. We try to negotiate but we can use formal notices if needed.

turns.speaker: Lord Redwood
turns.text: Can you give a concrete example where your intervention made a difference, with costs and benefits?

turns.speaker: Dame Helen Ghosh
turns.text: Our investigation into combined sewage outflows clarified the law where Defra, the Environment Agency, and Ofwat were confused. That changed their practice. Our waste inspections report exposed failures and we'll make sure promised improvements actually happen.

turns.speaker: Lord Jay of Ewelme
turns.text: You have powers to scrutinise, advise, and enforce. Will you put more emphasis on enforcement, and do you have enough powers?

turns.speaker: Dame Helen Ghosh
turns.text: We've achieved a lot by making failures transparent and suggesting practical fixes. The 'sub-nuclear' option is a decision notice, which we have used. We've never started an environmental review—a judicial review in effect—because it's costly and blunt. But I wouldn't rule it out, especially if there's disagreement on what the law means or the damage is severe.

chapters.title: Data gaps and water worries
chapters.takeaway: The OEP can't answer a specific question about pet parasite chemicals but flags the wider chemicals regime as a serious threat.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Our committee looked at pet parasite medications. Sales data for harmful chemicals is hidden as commercially sensitive. Could you help get that data?

turns.speaker: Natalie Prosser
turns.text: I can't answer that specific point, but we are concerned about how we regulate chemicals generally. We have a small amount of work looking at the chemicals regime. Chemicals present a material threat to the environment and our regulatory system may not be adequate.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Could you write to us about whether environmental law requires that data to be made available when chemicals are shown to be harmful?

turns.speaker: Baroness McIntosh of Pickering
turns.text: You've said progress has slowed and government is off track on its legal environmental commitments. Can you assess where we are now? What about the missing legally binding species targets?

turns.speaker: Dame Helen Ghosh
turns.text: Our report found government was off track on 21 out of 43 targets. The new plan is better on delivery plans but not perfect. We'll report again in January. I don't expect a big change. On species targets, I'll have to write to you.

turns.speaker: Baroness McIntosh of Pickering
turns.text: When we were in the EU, enforcement was effective. Is the current regime as strong? What work are you doing on the water framework directive?

turns.speaker: Dame Helen Ghosh
turns.text: We have an ongoing investigation into water framework directive implementation. It's already known from the Court of Appeal that government is failing its targets. We'll conclude this year. We're watching the water Bill, which may adjust the rules.

chapters.title: Targets, urgency, and biodiversity net gain
chapters.takeaway: Ministers are legally responsible for meeting environmental targets, but urgency is lacking, and the OEP is worried about biodiversity net gain being watered down.

turns.speaker: Earl Russell
turns.text: We're coming up against 2030 targets fast. If your work doesn't change government policy enough, what more can be done to get back on track?

turns.speaker: Dame Helen Ghosh
turns.text: We focus on outcomes, delivery plans, milestones, and transparency. We've had a generic effect across many issues and a detailed effect on the most salient ones. But we hear time's winged chariot hurrying near.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The OEP's chief scientist said it's still possible to meet the 2030 species target, but not acting is a choice to miss it. Do you sense government understands the urgency?

turns.speaker: Dame Helen Ghosh
turns.text: We need clarity on what a target really means. Ministers are responsible for meeting statutory targets. The only one we think is on a positive track is air quality.

turns.speaker: Natalie Prosser
turns.text: The framework is clear: responsibility sits with Ministers. Our role is to provide clear evidence of whether they're delivering.

turns.speaker: Lord Trees
turns.text: What's your assessment of biodiversity net gain? The consultation suggested exempting brownfield sites. And what about water use by data centres?

turns.speaker: Dame Helen Ghosh
turns.text: We're very worried about BNG being chipped away—exemptions for smaller sites, brownfield sites, and restrictions on local authorities. We've commented that the Planning Bill is regressive in legal terms. BNG hasn't had a chance to bed in.

turns.speaker: Natalie Prosser
turns.text: We need a broader water resources strategy. Data centres don't have to use water for cooling if the incentives are right. Water scarcity must be part of the water reforms.

chapters.title: Waste inspections and the Environment Agency
chapters.takeaway: The OEP's waste report found the Environment Agency's inspections deeply inadequate, but the agency is engaging and accepting the recommendations.

turns.speaker: Lord Rooker
turns.text: Your office was set up to replace EU fines after Brexit. How are you using that powerful tool? What's the Environment Agency's response to your waste report?

turns.speaker: Natalie Prosser
turns.text: We engaged with the Environment Agency before publishing. The report makes difficult reading on the quality of its inspections of regulated waste sites. They've engaged meaningfully and the response is imminent. I understand all our recommendations have broadly been accepted. There's work to do, but I'm confident.

turns.speaker: Lord Rooker
turns.text: Have you ever been contacted by a whistleblower from the Environment Agency?

turns.speaker: Natalie Prosser
turns.text: Yes, we've had whistleblowers from public authorities we oversee—four in the last reporting period.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Our committee found 38 million tonnes of waste illegally managed every year. The bulk comes from permitted sites regulated by the Environment Agency. What does that say about our regulator?

turns.speaker: Dame Helen Ghosh
turns.text: It's shocking. Our report on the new environmental plan will say the targets to reduce illegal waste lack ambition. We don't rule out looking at illegal waste tipping in future.

turns.speaker: Earl Russell
turns.text: The false positives from Environment Agency inspections were worrying. Are there lessons for other areas?

turns.speaker: Natalie Prosser
turns.text: Yes, there are whole-system issues: coherence, risk-based regulation, and variation in inspection approaches. We published a report on inspection regimes showing high variation. Lessons must be implemented.

chapters.title: Follow-ups, farming, and closing
chapters.takeaway: The OEP will follow up on court rulings and is pushing for a coherent approach to nature-friendly farming, not just the sustainable farming incentive alone.

turns.speaker: Lord Redwood
turns.text: What's your assessment of the water regulator's work on Thames Water?

turns.speaker: Natalie Prosser
turns.text: We haven't looked at Thames Water specifically. We did look at Ofwat's overall enforcement performance in our sewage investigation, and that drove a change in approach.

turns.speaker: Baroness Coffey
turns.text: Do you see a role in following up on court rulings, like the Pickering Fishery case?

turns.speaker: Dame Helen Ghosh
turns.text: Yes. The board recently discussed that it's not enough to publish a report or intervene in a case and move on. We need to make sure undertakings are fulfilled and outcomes improve. We'll build that into our strategy.

turns.speaker: Lord Trees
turns.text: You said nature-friendly farming is a priority. Have you fed into Defra's sustainable farming incentive scheme?

turns.speaker: Dame Helen Ghosh
turns.text: We're worried Defra is putting all its eggs in the SFI basket. It won't alone achieve the necessary improvements. Higher-tier schemes are underresourced. We're doing an informal report and a round table to gather views on the whole ecosystem.

turns.speaker: Natalie Prosser
turns.text: Defra has taken our recommendation seriously and we've seen greater transparency and coherence. The land use framework, farming profitability review, and farming road map are useful. Now it's about delivery.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you both for your time and openness. I draw this public session to a close.
